title: Event Sourcing & CQRS
subtitle: Follow one bank deposit as it is stored as an event, projected into a read model, and queried, and see why the read side lags.
learn: How storing events instead of current state keeps a full history
How current state is rebuilt by replaying a stream of events
Why CQRS splits the write model from one or more read models
Why the read side is eventually consistent and how to live with it
How snapshots keep command replay short, and how new projections are rebuilt from history

steps.title: The balance says 70. Why?
steps.body: A normal database keeps one row per account and overwrites it: balance = 70. The row cannot tell you how it got there, what it was last Tuesday, or whether a bug changed it. Event sourcing flips this. We store what happened (opened, deposited 100, withdrew 30) and treat the balance as something we compute. Here the store already holds three events for one account.
steps.idea: Keep the facts that happened; derive the current state from them.
steps.caption: Three events are stored; their sum is 70.

steps.title: Commands append events
steps.body: The client sends a command: deposit 50. The command service loads this account's events and replays them to get the current state (three events, balance 70), checks its rules, then appends a new Deposited event. The append says 'only if the stream is still at version 3'. If another writer got there first, the append is rejected and the command retries. Events are not edited in place; fixes are new events.
steps.idea: A command is validated against replayed state, then appends an immutable event with an expected version.
steps.caption: Command loads the stream, then appends event number 4.

steps.title: The gap before the read side
steps.body: The write is committed, but the screen your user reads from is a separate store. Asked for the balance right now, the read model has not heard about event 4 and still says 70. This is eventual consistency. With a push subscription the lag is often tens of milliseconds (our 40 ms is illustrative); a polling projector or a backlog can stretch it to seconds. To cope, the command can return the new stream version and the read waits until the read model reaches it, or the UI can show the new balance optimistically.
steps.idea: CQRS trades immediate read-after-write consistency for a separate, scalable read side; cope by waiting for the command's version or updating the UI optimistically.
steps.caption: A read sent right now returns the old balance.

steps.title: A projector builds the read model
steps.body: A projector subscribes to the event store, reads new events in order, and updates a table shaped for the screen. Deposited 50 becomes balance = 120 in the read model. The projector is just a consumer of the log. It remembers the last event number it applied, so after a crash it resumes from there and must be safe to re-apply an event it already saw.
steps.idea: A projection is a function over the event stream; it must be idempotent and restartable.
steps.caption: Event 4 flows to the projector and updates the read model.

steps.title: Queries never touch the events
steps.body: Now the same read returns 120. The query service reads one prepared row, with no replaying and no joins across event streams. The read model can sit in whatever store suits the question: a SQL table for account screens, a search index for transactions, a cache for dashboards. You can scale reads separately from writes, and add more read models without touching the write side.
steps.idea: Command Query Responsibility Segregation (CQRS) lets each side use the model and storage that fits its job.
steps.caption: Query service answers from the prepared read model.

steps.title: New question, new projection
steps.body: Product asks for monthly deposits per account, covering the last three years. With overwritten rows that data is gone. With events, you write a new projector and replay the whole history into a fresh read model while the old one keeps serving. Assume the whole store holds 50 million events across all accounts and the projector handles 20,000 per second: the rebuild takes about 40 minutes, then, once it catches up with events that arrived meanwhile, you switch traffic over.
steps.idea: Because events are the source of truth, any read model can be thrown away and rebuilt from scratch.
steps.caption: Whole history replayed into a brand new read model.

steps.title: A very long stream
steps.body: Replaying everything is fine for a projection that runs in the background. It is a problem on the write path. A busy account, say a merchant with 12,150 events, would have all of them loaded and folded on every command. At roughly 1 KB per event that is about 12 MB read per deposit, which turns a few-millisecond command into a slow one. Most streams are short; the long ones hurt.
steps.idea: Command latency grows with stream length unless you shorten what has to be replayed.
steps.caption: Each command now replays 12,150 events.

steps.title: Snapshots shorten the replay
steps.body: Every so often (say every 500 events) the service saves a snapshot: the aggregate's state plus the version it reflects. On the next command it loads the latest snapshot, then only the events after it. With a snapshot at version 12,000 it replays 150 events instead of 12,150. A snapshot is a cache, not the truth. If it is lost or its format changes, you rebuild it from the events.
steps.idea: A snapshot is saved state plus a version; load it, then replay only the tail.
steps.caption: Snapshot plus 150 newer events replaces 12,150.

steps.title: What you pay for this
steps.body: You gain history, audit, and rebuildable views. You pay in complexity. Old events live forever, so their shape must evolve carefully (versioned events, upcasters that translate old ones). Mistakes are fixed by appending a correcting event, not by editing. Personal data in immutable events complicates deletion requests; a common answer is encrypting per user and discarding the key. For plain CRUD screens, this is usually overkill.
steps.idea: Use event sourcing where history and audit matter; CQRS alone can be used without it.
steps.caption: Power of history versus cost of immutability.

steps.title: Facts in, views out
steps.body: Commands append immutable events guarded by an expected version. State is a fold over those events, shortened by snapshots. Projectors turn the log into read models shaped for queries, always slightly behind, so design screens and APIs for eventual consistency. Need a new view? Replay. Scaling reads? Add read models. Keep event sourcing for domains that benefit from history.
steps.idea: Write the truth once as events; derive every view from it.
steps.caption: Write side appends; read side projects and answers.

quiz.q: Two commands for the same account arrive at once, both after loading the stream at version 7. Each tries to append with 'expected version 7'. What should happen?
options: Both succeed and the events are merged
One append succeeds; the other is rejected and retries against the new state
The read model decides which one wins
quiz.why: The expected-version check is optimistic concurrency. Only one append can move the stream from 7 to 8; the loser must reload and re-validate, because its decision used stale state.

quiz.q: A user deposits money, is redirected to their account page, and sees the old balance. Refreshing a second later shows the new one. What is the best explanation and fix?
options: The projector had not applied the event yet; hand the UI the new version and let it wait or update optimistically
The event store dropped the event on write; add more replication to the store
The snapshots are stale for this account; take them more often than before
The query service is buggy; make it read straight from the event store
quiz.why: This is read-side eventual consistency. Fix it in the experience: hand the UI the command's new version and wait for the read model to reach it, or update the UI optimistically. Reading the event store for queries would throw away the point of CQRS.

quiz.q: You need a report no one planned for, covering all past activity. Why is that easy with event sourcing?
options: The write model can answer any query directly
Events are small, so scans are always fast
Replay the full event history through a new projector into a new read model
quiz.why: Events keep every recorded fact in order within each stream, so a new projection can be computed from the start, provided the events captured the data it needs. Overwritten state could not supply facts it never kept.

quiz.q: What is the correct role of a snapshot?
options: It replaces old events, which can then be deleted
It is a cached state at a known version that shortens replay; the events remain the source of truth
It keeps the read model consistent with the write model
It lets queries skip the projector
quiz.why: A snapshot speeds up loading an aggregate by starting from saved state. It can always be rebuilt from events, so it never replaces them.

cheatsheet.def: An immutable fact in past tense, such as Deposited 50. It is appended to a stream and treated as immutable.
The unit whose events are stored and replayed together, e.g. one account. Consistency rules are enforced inside one stream.
A check on append: only write if the stream is still at the version you loaded. Gives optimistic concurrency without locks.
Separate models for changing state (commands) and reading it (queries). Often paired with event sourcing, but usable without it.
A read model built by folding events into a shape suited to queries. Idempotent, restartable, and rebuildable by replay.
The read side trails the write side by a short, variable delay. Design reads, UIs and APIs to tolerate a stale view.
Saved aggregate state plus its version, taken every N events. Load it and replay only the tail. A cache, not the truth.
Translating old stored event versions to the current shape when reading, since events cannot be rewritten in place.
